chunks: First: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Hakim from Jamil ibn Darraj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from a man who gave something as a gift to his son, asking if it is permissible for him to take it back; he said: Yes, unless he is young.

Second: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan from Ibn Abi Umayr from Abd al-Rahman who said: I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who gave charity to some of his children while they were young, in the form of a female slave; then the slave pleases him while they are young dependents; do you think he can take her or appraise her at a fair price and witness against himself for its value, or leave it all and not deal with any of it? He said: He appraises her at a fair price, accounts for its value for them against himself, and takes her.

Third: As for what Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal narrated from al-Abbas ibn Amir from Dawud ibn al-Husayn from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: I asked him if anyone can take back charity or a gift; he said: As for what is given as charity for God's sake, no; as for the gift and the grant, he can take it back whether he has taken possession of it or not, even if it is for a relative.

Fourth: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Husayn from Safwan ibn Yahya who said: I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a man who had a debt from another man, so he gifted it to his son; the man mentioned the debt to him, so he said to him: There is nothing upon you regarding it in this world and the next, to please him, and he had indeed gifted it to one of his sons; he said: Yes, he gives it to him then revokes it and makes it a gift to this one; the meaning in these two narrations is that we interpret them as: if the children are adults, it is permissible for him to take back the gift; and we only prevented taking back what he gives to the young ones among them.

Fifth: As for what Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ibn Abi Nasr from Hammad from al-Mu'alla ibn Khunays who said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) if anyone can take back charity or a gift; he said: As for what is given as charity for God's sake, no; as for the gift and the grant, he can take it back whether he has taken possession of them or not, even if it is for a relative; the meaning in this narration is what we said in the first two narrations, equally.
ai.seo_question: Can a father take back a gift he gave to his children in Shia Islamic law?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi synthesizes seemingly contradictory reports by distinguishing between gifts to minors, which are irrevocable to protect their interest, and those to adults, which can be revoked even after possession. This juristic resolution highlights the Shia emphasis on the recipient's status and the distinction between *sadaqah* (charity) and *hiba* (gift), reflecting the broader legal principle that revocation is generally permitted unless specified otherwise. The discussion on compensating for a gifted slave girl underscores the practical application of fair valuation (*qiyamah*) in family transactions.
